lead: Email is a push then pull system. Your mail client pushes a message to your outgoing mail server over SMTP. That server pushes it to the receiver's mail server, which keeps it in a mailbox. Later the receiver's phone or laptop pulls the message out with POP3 or IMAP. This split exists because the two computers are rarely awake at the same time: the receiving server is always on, so it can hold mail. Every mail you send, from a UPI alert to an IRCTC ticket, follows this path.
prereq: You need: TCP sockets and ports from Chapter 6.2, DNS name lookup from Chapter 6.3, and the separate-control-and-data idea from Chapter 6.5.

blocks.text: Four pieces take part. The user agent (UA) is the program you type into: Gmail in a browser, Outlook, or a phone mail app. The mail server stores and forwards mail. Each user has a mailbox on a server, holding incoming messages, and an outgoing queue, holding messages not yet delivered.

Sending is a push. The UA opens a TCP connection to its own mail server and hands over the message. That server looks up the receiver's domain with DNS, finds the receiver's mail server, and opens a second TCP connection to push the message there. So SMTP runs twice: client to own server, then server to server.

If the second transfer fails, the message stays in the outgoing queue. The server retries later, often for a few days, then returns a bounce message to the sender. The receiver's UA never contacts the sender; it pulls from its own server. SMTP is push-only. It cannot ask a server for your mail. That is why a separate pull protocol exists.

sections.h3: SMTP commands, replies, and the 7-bit limit

blocks.text: SMTP is a text protocol on TCP port 25; port 587 is the submission port a mail client uses to hand over outgoing mail. The client sends commands, the server sends three-digit replies. A short session:

blocks.code:
S: 220 ready
C: EHLO client
S: 250 OK
C: MAIL FROM:<asha@example.in>
S: 250 OK
C: RCPT TO:<ravi@example.com>
S: 250 OK
C: DATA
S: 354 send message
C: Subject: Fee receipt
C: 
C: Body text
C: .
S: 250 queued
C: QUIT
S: 221 bye

blocks.text: EHLO opens the session and names the client. MAIL FROM gives the sender, RCPT TO gives one receiver (repeat for more), DATA starts the message, a line with a single dot ends it, and QUIT closes. Replies: 220 service ready, 250 command okay, 354 send the message, 550 no such mailbox or rejected. A 550 at RCPT TO makes the sender's server bounce the mail.

SMTP was built for 7-bit ASCII only: each character must fit in 7 bits. Photos, PDFs and Hindi text do not. MIME fixes this by adding headers. Content-Type says what the part is, such as image/jpeg or text/plain; charset=UTF-8. Content-Transfer-Encoding says how it was made ASCII-safe: base64 for binary, quoted-printable for mostly text. A multipart message uses a boundary string to separate parts.

blocks.where: original size is the binary attachment in bytes; encoded size is the base64 text in bytes, about one third larger.

blocks.text: Reading is a pull. POP3, TCP port 110, downloads messages to the client and usually deletes them from the server. It is simple and works offline, but a second device sees nothing. IMAP, TCP port 143, keeps mail on the server and synchronises folders, read and unread flags, and deletions across devices. Your phone and laptop show the same inbox.

figure.caption: The 6 KB of headers and text stays as it is, while the 300 KB photo grows to 400 KB after base64, so the Chennai-to-Delhi SMTP hop carries 406 KB. The phone then pulls that mail from the Delhi server with IMAP; SMTP only pushes.

spec.title: Push out, pull in
spec.aria: Four boxes in a row: the sender's client hands a 300 KB photo plus 6 KB of text to the sender's mail server, which base64-encodes the photo to 400 KB and pushes a total of 406 KB over SMTP port 25 to the receiver's mail server in Delhi, where the receiver's phone later pulls it with IMAP on port 143.

examples.question: An email has 6 KB of headers and text plus a 300 KB photo attached. Base64 adds one third to the photo. (a) Find the total size carried over the SMTP link. (b) The sender's server is in Chennai and the receiver's server in Delhi. Which protocol does the receiver's phone use to read the mail, and why not SMTP?
steps: The receiver pulls mail from the Delhi server using IMAP, or POP3 for a simple download. SMTP only pushes mail; it cannot fetch it.
examples.answer: The SMTP link carries 406 KB, and the receiver reads the mail with IMAP or POP3, never SMTP.
examples.check:
photo = 300
headers = 6
encoded = photo * 4 / 3
total = encoded + headers
print(int(encoded))
print(int(total))

traps: Using SMTP to fetch mail. SMTP only pushes; reading needs POP3 or IMAP.
Forgetting base64 expansion: a 300 KB photo becomes 400 KB on the wire, one third larger.
Mixing up ports: SMTP 25, submission 587, POP3 110, IMAP 143.
Thinking DATA ends at a blank line. It ends at a line containing only a single dot.
Assuming POP3 and IMAP are interchangeable: POP3 downloads and usually deletes, IMAP syncs state on the server.

quiz.q: Which protocol pushes mail between mail servers, and on which port?
quiz.a: SMTP, on TCP port 25. Mail clients submit outgoing mail on port 587.
SMTP carries only 7-bit ASCII. MIME adds Content-Type and Content-Transfer-Encoding headers so photos, PDFs and non-English text can be sent safely, using base64 or quoted-printable.

quiz.q: A 120 KB file is attached to a mail with 5 KB of headers and text. Base64 is used. What is the total size on the SMTP link?
A user reads the same mailbox on a phone and a laptop. Should the mail server offer POP3 or IMAP? Explain.
quiz.a: IMAP. It keeps mail on the server and syncs folders and read flags, so both devices see the same state. POP3 would download and usually delete messages, leaving the second device without them.

quiz.q: What does the SMTP reply 354 mean?
quiz.a: The server is ready to receive the message body; the client sends DATA and ends it with a line containing a single dot.

quiz.q: What happens at the sender's server when RCPT TO returns 550?
quiz.a: The receiver is rejected, for example no such mailbox. The server does not deliver; it later bounces the message back to the sender.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern mail uses SMTP with TLS, either SMTPS on port 465 or STARTTLS on port 587, plus authentication before submission. Webmail hides these protocols behind HTTPS to the browser, but the servers still speak SMTP, POP3 and IMAP. Search for MIME multipart, IMAP IDLE, and SMTP STARTTLS to go deeper.
